arguments.query: How did the North Harbor pilot change on-time performance, and what limitation does the report give on attributing that change to its interventions?
How did the North Harbor pilot change on-time performance, and what limitation does the report give on attributing that change to its interventions?

result.text: The on-time rate rose from 82 percent at baseline to 88 percent during the final four weeks. All-door boarding reduced median dwell time by 22 seconds at the three pilot stops. Bridge-related delays fell from 27 percent to 19 percent of tagged delays. The pilot was not randomized, so the report does not claim that the interventions alone caused the improvement.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: The review recommends keeping the spare bus procedure and recording dispatch response time for future ramp reports. It does not establish a fleet-wide ramp failure rate because the pilot covered only eight buses and 90 days.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot: Incident Review (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: The team trialed all-door boarding at the three busiest stops, added a four-minute schedule buffer before the bridge crossing, and introduced a signed handoff checklist for operators. These were operational changes; no passenger-level location history was collected.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: The North Harbor pilot ran on routes 4 and 7 for 90 days, from April through June 2026. It used eight buses and covered three high-volume stops. The baseline on-time rate was 82 percent.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: On May 18, one bus ramp stopped halfway through deployment during boarding. No one was injured. The driver used the accessible spare bus procedure, and dispatch sent a replacement vehicle 11 minutes after the report.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot: Incident Review (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: The final-week survey had 46 responses and was not representative of all riders. The report flags uncertainty about whether the new boarding process works equally well at crowded stops for wheelchair users. The next phase should include direct accessibility review before expansion.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot: Risk Register (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: The review found that the monthly maintenance checklist did not include a loaded ramp sensor check. The checklist was updated on May 25, and mechanics inspected all eight pilot buses by May 30. One sensor needed adjustment; the other seven passed.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot: Incident Review (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: Dispatch tagged 38 percent of recorded delays to long boarding queues, 27 percent to bridge openings, and 18 percent to operator handoffs. The remaining 17 percent had mixed or unknown causes. The tags came from 420 delayed trips.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot (fictional demonstration data)

result.text: The pilot used aggregate passenger counts from infrared door sensors. It did not collect names, payment identifiers, raw GPS trails, or device identifiers. Aggregate counts are retained for 30 days, then deleted. Access is limited to the transit analytics team.
result.title: North Harbor Bus Pilot: Risk Register (fictional demonstration data)
